title: Young people's mental health: self-harm, depression and eating disorders
blurb: Care for a young person after self-harm using NICE NG225, support stepped care for depression (NG134) and recognise eating disorders without relying on BMI (NG69).
question: Chloe, 14, is admitted to a children's ward overnight after a paracetamol overdose. She is medically stable. What arrangements should NICE NG225 put in place while she is on the ward?

teach.h: Mental health on a children's ward
teach.body: Children's nurses often meet young people in crisis on general wards, in emergency departments and in the community. Formally, NICE NG225 covers self-harm, NG134 depression in 5 to 18-year-olds and NG69 eating disorders. Plain English: treat the young person with respect, keep them physically safe, get specialist mental health input quickly, involve the family, and never reduce a person's risk to a score on a tool.

teach.h: On a paediatric ward after self-harm (NG225 1.7.24)
teach.caption: CYPMHS = children and young people's mental health services (CAMHS).

teach.body: NG225 says do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repeat self-harm, or to decide who gets treatment or who is discharged. Instead a mental health professional experienced with children and young people carries out a psychosocial assessment, asking about home, school, peer group, caring roles, social media and any safeguarding concerns. If the young person wants to leave first, assess their safety and mental health before they go.

teach.caption: Written with the young person and family, held by the young person, shared as they decide.

levels.label: Digital CBT, group CBT or support

head: Rule
Detail
teach.caption: Watch for increased agitation or suicidal thoughts after starting, and tell the family what to look for.

teach.note: FT-AN = anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy for children and young people.

teach.text: A 'normal' BMI centile does not rule out an eating disorder. Rapid weight loss, restriction and preoccupation with weight or shape matter, and NG69 says single measures such as BMI or how long the illness has lasted must not decide whether treatment is offered.

teach.h: Scenario: Ryan, 15, in the children's emergency department
teach.body: Ryan has cut his forearms and the wounds have been dressed. He is calm and says he wants to go home. Nurse Priya does not complete a risk score. She explains that a CYP mental health professional will see him, keeps him in a safe space, asks his permission to involve his mum, and tells the team he wants to leave so his safety and mental state are assessed before he goes. She treats him with the same respect as any other patient.

items: No risk tools or scales to predict repetition or decide treatment or discharge.
Paediatric ward after self-harm: 24-hour CYPMHS, joint daily review, daily family access, MDT.
Safety plans are written with, and held by, the young person.
Depression: watchful waiting reviewed within 2 weeks; fluoxetine offered in combination with psychological therapy.
Eating disorders: do not use BMI alone; consider FT-AN for anorexia in young people.

summary: You can now care for a young person after self-harm without relying on risk scores, help build a safety plan and set up the ward arrangements NG225 requires. You can also apply stepped care for depression and recognise and support eating disorders in line with NG69.

A.q: Chloe, 14, is on a children's ward after a paracetamol overdose and is medically stable. Which arrangement does NICE NG225 recommend while she is on the ward?
options: Weekly review by the mental health team
Joint daily review by paediatric and CYPMHS teams
Transfer to an adult psychiatric ward
A.why: NG225 1.7.24: joint daily review by the paediatric and CYP mental health teams, 24-hour CYPMHS access, daily family access and regular MDT meetings.

whyNot.0: Review should be daily and joint, not weekly.
whyNot.2: NG225 recommends daily access to family members or carers.
whyNot.3: Young people should be cared for in age-appropriate settings.

A.q: A nurse in the emergency department suggests using a risk scale to decide whether Amira, 13, can go home after self-harm. What does NG225 say?
options: Use the scale with a clinical interview
Use the scale if parents agree
Do not use scales to decide discharge
A.why: NG225: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict repetition or suicide, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged.

whyNot.0: Combining it with an interview does not make scale-based discharge decisions acceptable.
whyNot.1: Parental agreement does not change the recommendation.
whyNot.3: The recommendation applies at every age.

A.q: Ella, 15, was offered watchful waiting for mild depression. When should she be reviewed?
A.why: NG134: watchful waiting for mild depression includes a review within 2 weeks.

whyNot.1: Six weeks is too long for the planned review.
whyNot.2: Three months is far beyond the recommended review.
whyNot.3: Watchful waiting is an active plan with a set review, not waiting to be asked.

B.q: Josh, 16, has moderate to severe depression that has not responded to psychological therapy. Fluoxetine is being considered. Which plan matches NG134?
options: Fluoxetine with a review at 3 months
Fluoxetine with therapy and weekly contact
B.why: NG134: fluoxetine is offered together with concurrent psychological therapy, with weekly contact for the first 4 weeks.

whyNot.0: Fluoxetine is given with concurrent psychological therapy and weekly contact for the first 4 weeks, not a 3-month review.
whyNot.1: Paroxetine should not be used in this age group.
whyNot.3: Venlafaxine should not be used in this age group.

B.q: Mia, 14, has lost 6 kg in 3 months by restricting food and over-exercising. Her BMI centile is still in the healthy range. Her GP is unsure about referral. What does NG69 say?
options: Wait until her BMI falls below the 2nd centile
Offer dietary advice and review in a year
Refer once restriction has lasted 6 months
Do not use BMI alone to decide on treatment
B.why: NG69: do not use single measures such as BMI or duration of illness to decide whether to offer treatment. Rapid weight loss and restriction are warning signs.

whyNot.0: Waiting for a BMI threshold delays treatment.
whyNot.1: A year's delay ignores significant warning signs.
whyNot.2: Duration of illness is a single measure that should not decide treatment.

B.q: Leah, 13, has anorexia nervosa and will be treated in the community. Her parents ask which treatment is usually considered first. What does NG69 recommend?
B.why: NG69 1.3.10: consider anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy for children and young people (FT-AN).

whyNot.0: Medication is not the first-line treatment for anorexia.
whyNot.1: Family involvement is central for young people with anorexia.
whyNot.3: Community treatment is usual; admission is for medical or psychiatric need.

C.q: Ryan, 15, attends the emergency department after cutting his arms. His wounds are dressed. Before the CYP mental health practitioner arrives, he says he wants to leave. What should the nurse do?
options: Let him go with a leaflet and GP letter
Assess his safety and mental state first
Complete a risk scale to decide on leaving
Ask security to stop him from leaving
C.why: NG225 1.5.14: if a person wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment, assess their safety and any mental health problems before they leave.

whyNot.0: Leaving without any safety assessment is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Risk scales must not be used to decide discharge.
whyNot.3: Restraint is not the first step; a prompt safety assessment is.

C.q: Amira, 13, is going home after an overdose of her mother's tablets. A safety plan is being agreed. Which feature should it include?
options: A score showing her repeat risk
A plan held by the ward, not by Amira
A rule that she cannot use her phone
Ways to make her home environment safer
C.why: NG225 1.11.7: safety plans include keeping the environment safe by working together to remove or restrict means, alongside triggers, coping strategies and contacts.

whyNot.0: Risk scores are not used to predict repetition.
whyNot.1: The safety plan is held by the person.
whyNot.2: Blanket restrictions are not part of a collaborative safety plan.

C.q: Sophie, 15, has severe anorexia and is admitted to a paediatric ward for medical stabilisation and refeeding. Which guidance should the team use for medical risk and refeeding?
C.why: NG69 refers to the RCPsych MEED guidance for managing medical emergencies and refeeding in eating disorders.

whyNot.1: NG225 covers self-harm and recommends against risk tools.
whyNot.3: PEWS tracks deterioration but does not guide eating disorder refeeding (MEED = Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders).

reteach.title: Listen, plan, involve
reteach.question: How should a children's nurse respond to a young person in mental health crisis?

blocks.body: Listen: a psychosocial assessment by a CYP mental health professional, not a risk score. Plan: a safety plan written with the young person, including means restriction, triggers and contacts. Involve: family and the right team: CYPMHS daily on the ward, family therapy for anorexia, therapy alongside fluoxetine for depression.

blocks.text: 'Low risk' on a checklist is not a reason to discharge. NG225 asks for a needs-based psychosocial assessment instead.

explain.body: For children and young people, a mental health professional experienced with this age group assesses needs and safety, asking about home, school, peers, caring roles, social media and safeguarding.

test.q: Which topic does NG225 specifically list for the psychosocial assessment of a young person who has self-harmed?
options: Their use of social media and the internet
test.why: NG225 1.5.11 includes the use of social media and the internet, alongside social, peer, education, home, caring roles and safeguarding.

whyNot.2: Education is asked about, but not a 5-year grade history.
whyNot.3: Parents' medical history is not a listed area.

explain.body: A young person admitted to a paediatric ward after self-harm should have 24-hour CYPMHS access, a joint daily paediatric and mental health review, daily family access and regular MDT meetings.

test.q: How often should paediatric and CYP mental health teams jointly review a young person admitted after self-harm?
test.why: NG225 1.7.24 recommends a joint daily review.

whyNot.1: Twice weekly is not the recommendation.
whyNot.3: Review is daily throughout the admission.

explain.body: Fluoxetine is the antidepressant offered to young people with moderate to severe depression, with concurrent psychological therapy and weekly contact for the first 4 weeks. Paroxetine, venlafaxine and tricyclics are not used.

test.q: Which antidepressant should not be offered to a young person with depression under NG134?
test.why: NG134: do not use paroxetine, venlafaxine or tricyclic antidepressants for depression in children and young people.

whyNot.2: Sertraline is a later option in NG134 if fluoxetine is not effective.
whyNot.3: Citalopram is a later option in NG134 if fluoxetine is not effective.

explain.body: Warning signs include rapid weight loss, restrictive eating, disproportionate concern about weight or shape, faltering growth and delayed puberty. Do not use BMI or illness duration alone to decide on treatment.

test.q: Which finding in a 12-year-old can be a sign of an eating disorder, according to NG69?
test.why: NG69: children and young people with eating disorders may present with faltering growth or delayed puberty.

whyNot.0: A growth spurt is normal development.
whyNot.2: Early puberty is not listed as an eating disorder sign.
whyNot.3: Increased appetite alone is not a listed warning sign.
